extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states the conceptual standards and distinctions for classifying capital, interest, profits, and the modes of production, and explains the law determining the rate of interest and its relation to wages and rent. Geared to interpretation and application of 19th‑century political‑economic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Production falls into three modes—ADAPTING, or changing natural products either in form or in place so as to fit them for the satisfaction of human desire; GROWING, or utilizing the vital forces of nature, as by raising vegetables or animals; EXCHANGING, or utilizing, so as to add to the general sum of wealth, the higher powers of those natural forces which vary with locality, or of those human forces which vary with situation, occupation, or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the first mode capital may aid labor but is not absolutely necessary; in the second and third modes capital must aid labor. The character of capital's contribution differs: in ADAPTING the benefit is in the use; in GROWING the benefit is in the increase; in EXCHANGING the benefit is in the increase or greater value of the things received in return. These distinctions underpin later claims about how returns are distributed between labor and capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of capital (tangible wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be capital ... that is not wealth—that is to say, nothing can be capital that does not consist of actual, tangible things, not the spontaneous offerings of nature, which have in themselves, and not by proxy, the power of directly or indirectly ministering to human desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital is 'wealth applied in a certain way'—a form of labor impressed on matter. This standard excludes intangible claims that do not correspond to existing tangible wealth from being treated as genuine capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government bonds and evidences of indebtedness not capital per se
rubrics_metrics.description: A government bond is not capital, nor yet is it the representative of capital. The capital that was once received for it by the government has been consumed unproductively ... The bond cannot represent capital that has been destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Securities represent capital only insofar as they actually correspond to capital presently existing and applied to productive uses (e.g., bonds issued for infrastructure that created lasting capital). Otherwise they are promises to transfer future wealth (taxation) and their interest payments are effectively taxes on present produce, not returns of real capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictitious or overissued capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one dollar’s worth of capital has been really used, certificates for two, three, four, five, or even ten, have been issued ... upon this fictitious amount interest or dividends are paid with more or less regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returns paid on amounts in excess of real capital invested are not true interest; such surplus payments should be classified as wages of superintendence or other non‑interest receipts. The existence of fictitious capital distorts the distribution of real productive returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and nature of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest springs from the power of increase which the reproductive forces of nature, and the in effect analogous capacity for exchange, give to capital. It is not properly a payment made for the use of capital, but a return accruing from the increase of capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest is a return arising from time‑element increases (e.g., planted corn, cattle maturing, exchanges yielding gains over time). It should be understood as a natural, not arbitrary or purely social, phenomenon tied to reproduction and time, which makes it 'just' in the author's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between benefits of use and benefits of increase
rubrics_metrics.description: Primarily, the benefits which arise from use go to labor, and the benefits which arise from increase, to capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modes of production correlate and society averages returns across modes, the ultimate division of produce subtracts from each source enough to allow both labor and capital their competitive returns. This 'averaging' explains how returns are shared in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spurious profits mistaken for interest (monopoly, superintendence, speculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits thus derived [from monopoly, protective tariffs, patents, combinations, concentrated capital, etc.] are not to be confounded with the legitimate returns of capital as an agent of production ... wages of superintendence ... and profits properly due to the elements of risk are frequently confounded with interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: exclusive privileges (patents, royal grants), protective tariffs, railroad or telegraph combinations, and speculative gains (stock‑dealing) produce receipts commonly called interest but arising from monopoly, managerial skill, or risk‑taking, and should be separately classified when analyzing returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of capital creates monopoly power and non‑interest returns
rubrics_metrics.description: In the aggregation of large masses of capital under a common control there is developed a new and essentially different power ... a power of the same kind as that which James granted to Buckingham ... often exercised with as reckless a disregard ... Every one knows the tyranny and rapacity with which capital when concentrated in large amounts is frequently wielded to corrupt, to rob, and to destroy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such concentrated power yields profits that are not the constructive increase of capital but destructive/extractive returns attributable to bad legal/social adjustments; these must be distinguished from true interest when assessing sources of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest is not merely 'payment for use' but a natural return tied to time
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest is not properly a payment made for the use of capital, but a return accruing from the increase of capital. Whoever uses capital and obtains the increase it is capable of giving receives interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: planting a tree yields fruit (interest) on the capital embodied in the tree; using one's own machinery to produce yields an advantage equivalent to interest. Conversely, charging for the mere deferral of payment without corresponding increase is not true interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital is produced by labor; capital is not fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is not a fixed quantity, but can always be increased or decreased, (1) by the greater or less application of labor to the production of capital, and (2) by the conversion of wealth into capital, or capital into wealth, for capital being but wealth applied in a certain way, wealth is the larger and inclusive term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion implies政策 implications: changes in incentives for producing capital or consuming it alter the available capital stock and thus the returns to capital and labor. It also grounds the view that capital and labor are forms of the same human exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium relation between wages and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be such a point ... at, or rather, about, which the rate of interest must tend to settle; since, unless such an equilibrium were effected, labor would not accept the use of capital, or capital would not be placed at the disposal of labor. ... Hence interest must rise and fall with the rise and fall of wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under free competition the reward of capital and the reward of labor will be equalized so each yields an equally attractive result for exertion; disturbances push labor into capital production or wealth into capital uses to restore equilibrium. This is a general (not case‑by‑case) law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal rate of interest determined by average power of increase and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal point of interest ... will be determined by the strength of these [reproductive] forces and the extent to which they are engaged in production ... this normal point of interest ... must ... be such that all things (such as the feeling of security, desire for accumulation, etc.) considered, the reward of capital and the reward of labor will be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reproductive forces vary, market mechanisms (value adjustments, extension of exchange) produce an equilibrium average increase of capital that fixes a typical/normal interest rate between replacement and maximum possible return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest determined by the margin of cultivation (corollary of law of rent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of flour ... by saying that the general rate of interest will be determined by the return to capital upon the poorest land to which capital is freely applied—that is to say, upon the best land open to it without the payment of rent. Thus we bring the law of interest into a form which shows it to be a corollary of the law of rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This offers a practical way to compute or reason about general interest: interest falls as rent increases (all else equal); in extreme cases where capital could produce wealth without labor, increasing rent would absorb most returns, leaving little for interest.
